results.title: Compute Is Becoming a Tradable Commodity — and Wall Street Is Racing to Build the Market — On The Wire
highlights:
Compute futures apply that idea to renting GPUs — the chips that train and run AI models. And the problem they're built to solve is real. According to the research firm SemiAnalysis, the price of renting an Nvidia H100 on a one-year contract climbed nearly 40% in five months, from a low of around $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to roughly $2.35 by March 2026. Spot prices swing even more wildly — depending on the provider and how long you commit, an H100 today can cost anywhere from about $1.50 to over $11 an hour, with the market median somewhere near $3.

For a lab planning a months-long training run, that volatility is brutal. A compute future lets it lock in a price now; if GPU rental rates rise, the gain on the contract offsets the higher bill. Cloud and data-centre operators want the mirror image — predictable revenue to justify the enormous sums they're spending on chips and power. As CME's chairman Terry Duffy put it, "Compute is the new oil of the 21st century… Investors need a trusted futures market to provide transparency, liquidity and effective risk management."

...

CME and Silicon Data will base their contracts on Silicon Data's "Silicon Index," a daily benchmark of H100 and A100 rental rates captured across cloud providers and recalculated every business day. Silicon Data is backed by the trading firm DRW, whose founder Don Wilson predicts "compute will become the largest commodity in the world." The contracts are expected to be cash-settled to that index, with a launch planned for later this year pending regulatory review.

ICE and Ornn take a different tack. Their contracts reference the Ornn Compute Price Index, which Ornn says is the first compute benchmark built only from printed transactions — actual executed trades, rather than surveyed rates. The contracts are dollar-denominated and cash-settled, and would cover a wider spread of chips: H100, H200, B200 and even the RTX 5090. The survey-based-versus-transaction-based distinction is the crux of a genuine debate about which method better reflects the true price of compute.

...

The timing isn't a coincidence. The whole industry is short of compute, and everyone expects that to continue. Days before any of these deals went public, BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink told the Milken Institute conference that "a new asset class will be buying futures of compute," arguing the US simply doesn't have enough chips, memory and power for the AI workloads coming. He turned out to be describing something that was already weeks from launch.

That's the real signal here. You don't build a futures market for something you think is a passing shortage. You build one when you believe scarcity is a permanent, structural feature of the economy — durable enough to underwrite a whole layer of financial machinery on top of it.

...

The biggest is fungibility. A barrel of crude oil is a barrel of crude oil. A "GPU-hour" is not nearly so uniform: its real value depends on the chip model, how the cluster is wired together, the maturity of the software, storage, even geography. Two clusters with the same nominal H100-hours can deliver meaningfully different output. Critics argue that makes compute a "fake commodity" — a marketing proxy that hides too much variance to price cleanly. Notably, Silicon Data's own chief executive, Carmen Li, has publicly acknowledged that fungibility challenges complicate trading.

Then there's obsolescence. Oil doesn't go out of date; GPUs do, fast. The H100 is already being succeeded by the H200 and Blackwell chips, which raises a hard question about what a contract dated a year out is even referencing. And there's the basic liquidity problem: no one yet trades a standardised "1,000 H100-hours, US-East, third quarter" contract, and a market only works if enough buyers and sellers show up.

results.title: REIT + Bitcoin, GPU Shortage — Daily Report, Jun 20, 2026
highlights:
Podcasts today converged on a single structural tension: AI and automation are driving concentrated capital flows and real, near‑term supply constraints while policy and macro risks still threaten to reprice those bets. Guests from MacroMinds and Odd Lots highlighted concrete supply pressures — GPU rental prices up roughly 40–50% since January and DRAM/NAND demand/prices up roughly 4–5x — that justify continued capex and elevated valuations in suppliers even as market internals remain narrow. At the same time, Thoughtful Money and other panels flagged policy uncertainty (the new Fed chair's 2% pledge and five task forces on real‑time data) plus calendar/technical risks (record quadruple‑witching, pension rebalancing) that could trigger a sharp, short‑term correction around the August–October midterm window. The day’s loudest, most actionable claims: (1) memory and GPU scarcity are not theoretical — speakers gave numeric evidence (4–5x DRAM/NAND surge; GPUs +40–50% rental spikes) that underpins multi‑year capex plans and distributor profits; (2) corporate and retail behavior is amplifying risk — H1 2026 retail/ETF inflows and record margin debt vs M2 concentrate exposure in leveraged tech and semis; and (3) new funding and structuring innovations (one sponsor’s six deals totaling ~ $1bn with ~$200m of Bitcoin, and examples embedding three BTC per apartment in a 366‑unit purchase) are changing balance‑sheet liquidity for illiquid assets, even as the 1965 REIT law’s ~90% distribution rule remains a structural constraint. Together these forces create a mixed market: strong structural tailwinds for AI suppliers but elevated timing, policy and technical risks for broad equity exposure.

...

GPU Shortage — MacroMinds guests reported exploding token usage tightened GPU capacity and pushed rental prices up roughly 40–50% since January, creating immediate scarcity that supports incremental supplier pricing power.

...

Memory Surge — Speakers quantified DRAM/NAND demand and prices rising roughly 4–5x driven by datacenter AI and said elevated memory needs could persist for ~2–4 years, arguing market pricing that expects a 6–9 month rollover (forward multiples near 6–7) is likely premature.

results.title: Silicon Data and CME Group Partner to Launch World's First AI Compute Futures Contracts · TechEchelon
highlights:
Silicon Data has partnered with CME Group to develop the first futures contracts tied to AI computing power costs, giving companies a potential tool to hedge against GPU rental-rate volatility. The contracts are still awaiting CFTC approval.

...

A startup that tracks pricing across cloud providers and GPU marketplaces has partnered with one of the world's largest derivatives exchanges to create futures contracts tied to the cost of artificial intelligence computing power — a move that could give companies a financial tool to hedge against swings in what has become one of their most volatile operating expenses.

Silicon Data has teamed with CME Group to develop what the companies describe as the first futures contracts benchmarked to AI compute costs. The contracts are still awaiting regulatory approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The underlying premise mirrors how airlines manage jet fuel exposure. Most companies using AI do not own the high-end graphics processing units required to train and run models. Instead, they rent access through cloud providers and a growing tier of so-called neoclouds — and those rental rates fluctuate, complicating financial planning.

"Right now we're at a high point of uncertainty," said Seoyoung Kim, a finance professor at Santa Clara University. "A lot of people don't know how much computing power they'll need in the next year, and a lot of suppliers of that computing power right now don't know how many GPUs and to what capacity they should order and the manufacturers, like Nvidia, they don't know how much they should produce."

Silicon Data has built a set of GPU price indexes that track the hourly rental cost of specific chips across multiple providers. The company intends those benchmarks to serve as the foundation of a futures market, in the same way West Texas Intermediate crude oil underpins energy derivatives.

...

Standardization represents a significant technical and regulatory hurdle. Unlike a barrel of crude oil, AI compute is not a uniform physical commodity. Silicon Data said there are more than 50 different configurations of Nvidia's H100 chip alone, with prices varying by processor type, memory, networking, utilization rates, and data center location.

...

If the contracts clear regulatory review, they would give both compute buyers and sellers a mechanism to lock in pricing — buyers seeking protection from rising costs, providers hedging against a potential drop in rates. How quickly those two sides of the market develop, and whether sufficient liquidity follows, will determine whether AI compute ultimately earns a place alongside oil, corn, and metals on the derivatives trading floor.

results.title: iFAST Global Markets | Fintech Powered One-Stop Wealth Management Platform
highlights:
## Vera Rubin | Pricing Through the Lens of GPU Rental Price

Beyond the near-flat capex per watt, a second way to judge whether NVIDIA is pricing with restraint is GPU rental. First, distinguish two prices and two parties: NVIDIA sells the complete VR NVL72 system to cloud providers (Neoclouds) at a system price; the Neoclouds in turn rent compute to customers such as AI labs on a per-GPU-per-hour basis — the GPU rental. Because the system price is the Neocloud’s largest cost, the rental is a useful window onto NVIDIA’s pricing.

A cost-based rental floor. Neoclouds will buy and deploy the newest product only if it earns at least the return of the prior generation. Per SemiAnalysis, NVIDIA’s last generation delivered a project IRR of about 15.6% (assuming a five-year useful life and a 15% customer prepayment). On that basis the rental floor for the VR NVL72 is USD 4.92 per GPU-hour; below it, Neoclouds earn less than 15.6% and have little incentive to deploy. This floor floats with NVIDIA’s system price — the more NVIDIA charges, the higher the Neocloud’s cost and the higher the required floor.

A value-based ceiling. The ceiling is set by the customer’s alternatives. What customers really buy is compute, so the metric they care about most is cost per unit of compute. Because Vera Rubin produces far more compute per hour than the GB300, even a higher hourly rental can still be cheaper per PFLOP. Per SemiAnalysis the rental ceiling is about USD 12.25 per GPU-hour; above that, the customer’s cost per unit of compute would exceed the prior-generation GB300, so the rental cannot go higher.

Raising the system price lifts the Neocloud’s procurement cost, and to keep its ~15.6% target IRR the Neocloud must pass some of it on as higher rental. But for its customers — the AI labs — what matters is not whether the rental rises, but that the compute bought at a given price is no less than before. So as long as Rubin’s cost per unit of compute stays below the GB300’s, the labs still have reason to accept a higher rental. NVIDIA’s pricing, therefore, sits between two bounds: a floor set by the return Neoclouds need, and a ceiling set by what the labs will accept while keeping cost per unit of compute no higher than the prior generation. Since Neoclouds have limited pricing power, this is essentially a value-split between NVIDIA and the AI labs — the closer the rental to the floor, the more of the performance gain the labs enjoy; the closer to the ceiling, the more NVIDIA and the Neoclouds recapture.

Table 2: VR NVL72 Rental Pricing Framework (5-Year Contract, 15% Prepayment)

Note: GB300 is the baseline. “VR at current price” ≈ the cost-based floor (the minimum rental at which Neoclouds match the GB300 return hurdle); the value-based ceiling is the rental at which customer cost per unit of compute equals the GB300. 

Source: SemiAnalysis AI TCO Model and iFAST Compilation.

Rubin is not without room to raise prices — NVIDIA simply has not fully exercised it. At today’s system price, assuming Neoclouds keep their IRR of 15.6%, implied rental sits closer to the USD 4.92 floor than the USD 12.25 ceiling, so most of the economic value from Rubin’s performance leap currently accrues to model-side customers. Per SemiAnalysis, NVIDIA could lift system prices significantly, and customers would still enjoy below-trend improvements in cost per unit of compute, while Neoclouds would retain room to raise rentals and earn higher returns. In other words, this is a market where everyone is making money, and no one is charging what they could.

The rental could be pushed toward the ceiling, yet today it sits near the floor. Why is NVIDIA so restrained? We see four considerations. 

First, ecosystem lock-in over short-term gain: NVIDIA’s true moat is its complete hardware-software ecosystem, and pricing too aggressively this early could slow adoption, push the largest hyperscalers to accelerate their own ASICs, or encourage Neoclouds to embrace alternatives such as AMD — eroding share and pricing power over time. 

Second, the trade-off between demand elasticity and adoption speed: Vera Rubin is only just shipping, and NVIDIA would rather lift total profit through high volumes and share gains than maximise unit price on a single platform, much as it did early in the Blackwell cycle. 

Third, NVIDIA may simply be pricing too conservatively: its logic still seems anchored in the old chip-cycle assumption that compute keeps getting cheaper, not yet fully reflecting how agentic AI has repriced tokens higher — so it may be underestimating the model labs’ willingness to pay for efficient compute. 

Fourth, avoiding downstream backlash and regulatory risk: the GPU sticker price is the single most scrutinised number in the industry, and aggressive hikes amid a supply shortage invite collective pushback or antitrust attention — which is why NVIDIA instead leans on the quieter SOCAMM memory-pricing lever, covered in depth in " Memory Supercycle | AI Tokenomics and the Next Memory Repricing Opportunity".
